questions.question: Describe the position of skilled white workers on the Witwatersrand and explain why they demanded a colour bar.
questions.expected_answer: Deep-level mining needed skills in shaft sinking, timbering, blasting and running engines, found among miners from Cornwall, Australia and the United States, who emigrated in the 1880s and 1890s for high wages. They were few, hard to replace, earned many times black wages, lived with families in town, and formed unions such as the Transvaal Miners' Association in 1902. They faced miners' phthisis from rock dust, with many drillers dying young, and the threat that owners would replace them with cheaper black workers who learned the same skills. They demanded a colour bar reserving jobs for whites, set by custom and agreements and by law, such as the Mines and Works Act of 1911 restricting certificates of competency. It protected white jobs but blocked black workers from skilled work and wages.

questions.question: Explain the poor white problem and how mine owners and governments responded.
questions.expected_answer: Afrikaner families lost their place on the land as farms were subdivided, bywoners were pushed off by commercial farming, rinderpest in 1896 to 1897 killed most cattle, droughts struck and the South African War of 1899 to 1902 destroyed farms. Thousands moved to towns, especially Johannesburg, with little education, industrial skill or English. Unskilled mine work was done by black workers at very low wages, and owners would not pay whites more for the same work, creating a group of white people in poverty. Governments and churches saw this as a political danger and responded with relief works, training and later the civilised labour policy reserving some jobs for whites at higher wages. Mine owners found unskilled whites too expensive and instead imported about 63 000 Chinese indentured workers from 1904 to 1907, sent back by 1910, which white workers and voters strongly opposed.

questions.question: Describe the anti-Indian laws passed between 1885 and 1907 and explain why they were passed.
questions.expected_answer: White settlers, especially traders competing with Indian traders, demanded restrictions as ex-indentured and passenger Indians settled, bought land and traded. South African Republic Law 3 of 1885: land ownership only in set streets, wards and locations, registration and a fee, no citizenship. Orange Free State 1891: Indians effectively banned except as labourers. Natal: 1895 annual tax of three pounds on ex-indentured Indians who stayed without re-indenturing or returning, applying to men, women and older children; 1896 franchise law removing Indians from the voters' roll; 1897 Immigration Restriction Act with a European-language test, and the Dealers' Licences Act allowing councils to refuse licences. Transvaal 1907 Asiatic Registration Act, the Black Act, requiring registration with fingerprints, which led to Gandhi's satyagraha campaign. The laws protected white economic interests and reflected racial attitudes, and laid foundations for segregation.
